title: AI Is Redrawing the Map of the US-China Rivalry
author: Hal Brands
summary: Hal Brands 认为 AI 正在重塑大国竞争的战略地理。目前 AI 生态仍是美国优势格局：顶尖模型在美国，关键零部件来自台湾、日本、韩国、荷兰等盟友。但 AI 正推动一种不均衡的中美两极，模糊了尖端创新与战争前线的边界，抬高了非洲、南美等被华盛顿忽视地区的价值，同时让部分支撑美国技术优势的同盟关系承压。

paragraphs.text: Technology is always changing; geography is far more constant. But innovation continually remakes the world’s strategic geography — the meaning and value of key terrain.

Breakthroughs in sail and later steam brought an age of European global dominance. The internal combustion engine made the Middle East a jackpot and a tinderbox. The nuclear revolution cemented a Cold War order dominated by rival superpowers. The revolutionary technology of our era, artificial intelligence, is changing the strategic environment once more.

In many ways, the world’s AI ecosystem reflects a geography of US advantage. American labs make the world’s best models. Critical components come from close US allies and security partners around the Eurasian rim: Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, the Netherlands and others.
That’s not just a coincidence: For decades, America’s security network has nourished a community of dynamic nations. The prize is a landscape of innovation that reinforces US power.

Yet in ways both profound and subtle, AI is shifting the strategic topography. That technology is encouraging the advent of a messy, uneven bipolarity between the US and China. It is shaking up relations between states and non-state actors; it’s creating dangerous overlap between the terrain of high-end innovation and the geography of modern war. The development of AI challenges US diplomacy by highlighting the importance of areas Washington has underemphasized, such as Africa and South America — while also, paradoxically, straining some of the alliances that enhance America’s geo-technological power.

The geography of AI innovation is still a landscape of American advantage. But the threats to that advantage are mounting, and the global terrain becomes more challenging, as AI redraws the strategic map.
The AI Stack Is Global

The fact of that revolution is undeniable; its speed and impact have become astounding. Just this year, we’ve seen groundbreaking wartime uses of AI in conflicts in Iran and Venezuela. Leading models have emerged as cutting-edge tools of cyberwarfare. As AI capabilities race forward, so do fears of the havoc that poorly trained or rogue agents might create. The US and China have thus talked AI safety at two great-power summits, even as President Donald Trump touts the technology as the essential source of future wealth and strength.

Yet top AI models don’t magically appear; they’re built atop a complex foundation of inputs. These include cutting-edge semiconductors, extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, advanced design tools and chemical processes. Access to energy, capital and talent is also part of the mix. This collection of resources makes up the global AI stack — and, in many ways, it showcases US strengths.

American labs, such as Anthropic and OpenAI, produce the best frontier models. Most bleeding-edge semiconductors are designed in the US and fabricated in Taiwan. South Korea, Japan and Singapore play crucial roles in the semiconductor ecosystem. So does ASML, in the Netherlands, as the world’s sole producer of EUV machines. Other North Atlantic Treaty Organization allies, such as France and the UK, make important contributions to AI supply chains. In the Persian Gulf, two quasi-US allies — Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — have emerged as hubs for the data-center clusters that the AI buildout demands.

The AI stack is a testament to the intricacies of globalization and the achievements of the geopolitical network America has led since World War II. By securing the vital Eurasian rimlands, the US nurtured prosperous, innovative societies. Today, the US alliance system provides reliable access to many — not all — of the crucial inputs that drive America’s AI development, as well as leverage that helps it hold its rivals back.

For years, the US has placed curbs on China’s access to AI chips and the equipment needed to make them. It has exploited the strategic influence its alliance system offers to nudge key actors such as Japan and the Netherlands to impose restrictions of their own. America’s allies were helping a “villain do evil” by inhibiting Beijing’s AI sector, one Chinese official fumed in 2023. Yet if the AI stack delivers persistent US advantage, innovation is also shifting the contours of global power.
China Is Cheating to Win

For one thing, the US isn’t the sole center of strength in the AI era — new technology is hastening the shift to a more bipolar world. Yes, America retains an important lead over China in the sophistication of its models and the computing power needed to deploy them. This isn’t a rivalry between equals: Beijing has made itself a fast follower partly by reverse-engineering the achievements of US firms.

But cheating is just a form of competing: Through means fair or foul, Chinese firms have built impressive frontier models. Beijing seeks to win the future by diffusing Chinese open-weight models globally and using AI-driven breakthroughs to turbocharge its economy. Its strengths — from its chokehold on rare-earth elements to its scientific and engineering talent — are real.

Two great powers are competing for AI dominance, with the rest of the field far behind. Yet if this new bipolarity is unbalanced, it’s also messy, thanks to linkages and dependencies the AI stack creates.

Dreams of self-reliance aside, the US and China still need inputs they must access through a contested world economy. At the moment, they can’t even escape dependence on each other. A Chinese rare-earth embargo would throttle US data-center construction; tighter US export controls could constrict flows of capital and technology to Chinese firms.
A map of the US and Chinese AI ecosystems doesn’t depict self-contained blocs; it reveals insecure interdependence on both sides.

In fact, the US and Chinese techno-spheres overlap. Chinese open-weight AI models have proven attractive not simply in poorer, developing countries, but also in advanced economies where businesses seek enterprise solutions without breaking the bank. When I visited Japan over the summer, one senior official told me he worried that Chinese models would prove “extremely contagious” within the US alliance system. Or perhaps even in America: When the US firm Hugging Face was hacked by OpenAI agents in July, it used a Chinese model to help analyze and understand the attack.

Looking ahead, many countries may have ties to both the US and Chinese techno-spheres. At the same time, actors that can’t compete at the frontier — India, Singapore, the European Union — are making “middle-power” AI plays meant to strengthen sovereignty and avoid outright dependence on Washington or Beijing.
At some point, US-China tensions could cause a harder techno-fragmentation. But so far, the emerging landscape is one in which geopolitical splits and technological connections go hand in hand.
Companies Compete With Countries

International competition doesn’t happen solely among governments. Nations share the strategic terrain with other entities, from legitimate corporations to terrorist organizations and drug cartels. AI is poised to unsettle the landscape of power by shifting how interactions involving both state and non-state actors play out.

Today’s top AI firms are mighty, semi-sovereign actors. Their influence can be curbed by governments: Witness the Pentagon’s crackdown on Anthropic earlier this year, or the expectation that leading Chinese firms will heed directives from Beijing. But a core difference between now and the Cold War is that vital instruments of competition are held in private hands.

That dynamic could make leading labs strategically indispensable. It certainly makes the relationship between companies and the state — whether functional or dysfunctional, adversarial or cooperative — a core determinant of national power. It also raises the possibility that private actors could trigger a global crisis: Imagine that the OpenAI agents that escaped their sandbox in the Hugging Face incident had hacked important Chinese assets instead.

Equally worrying scenarios involve AI empowering terrorist groups that use sophisticated models to build bioweapons or drug cartels that use AI to perfect their distribution networks. In the near future, writes Vanda Felbab-Brown of the Brookings Institution, “Swarms of marine surface or close-to-surface drones equipped with AI-powered adaptive navigation systems will be launchable from a fishing ship just at the edge of an exclusive economic zone of a country to ferry drugs ashore.”

The pendulum won’t swing in just one direction: Law-enforcement authorities could use AI-enabled intelligence tools to map and dismantle cartel hierarchies. But for now, non-state actors are becoming more potent — which will make global networks of influence more fluid.
Virtual Weapons, Real War

At the same time, the landscape of innovation is becoming deeply entangled with the landscape of conflict. Key nodes of the global AI stack sit on dangerous geopolitical fault lines, vastly raising the technological cost of modern war.

In February, the US and Israel launched an AI-backed aerial assault against Iran and its leaders. Tehran responded, in part, by hitting data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates — and by threatening to attack facilities associated with US tech giants throughout the Persian Gulf.

Iran deemed these installations legitimate targets in a war in which AI was a major force-multiplier. Its strikes showed how the cramped geography and violent politics of the region can threaten vital infrastructure the AI buildout demands.

A war over Taiwan would be exponentially more traumatic. The output of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company powers America’s leading AI models, an asymmetric advantage for Washington because Chinese firms can’t legitimately access TSMC’s best chips. But geography gives China an asymmetric ability to hold that supply at risk.

A Chinese attack on Taiwan wouldn’t just derange the balance of power in the Western Pacific. It could also leave a smoking ruin at the heart of the AI ecosystem on which the US and so many other countries depend.
These risks create crosswinds for US policy. Tech reliance may deepen American commitment to endangered partners: If not for the AI connection, Trump would surely care less about Taiwan’s fate.

But dependence on imperiled assets may also encourage diversification, as difficult as that process can be: Taiwan’s precarious position is one reason recent presidents have emphasized building more advanced fabrication plants in the US. Or perhaps the future holds even more ambitious efforts to lift data centers and other infrastructure above the landscape of conflict — by placing them in outer space.
Beijing’s Material Advantage

For now, the AI stack remains thoroughly terrestrial, and it reflects geographies of power that are historically familiar for Washington. Yet the AI buildout is also compelling new patterns of engagement, in places where America has, frequently, underinvested and is now racing to catch up.

AI requires critical minerals that aid semiconductor manufacturing and large energy-storage systems. That gives China, with its dominance of rare-earth extraction and processing, a crucial chokepoint. It also advantages countries like the Democratic Republic of Congo, the world’s cobalt hyperpower; Indonesia and the Philippines, with their nickel; and Argentina and Chile, with their lithium. Don’t forget Kazakhstan, whose reserves of oil, gas and uranium power its ambitions to become a data-center hub.

The US is well positioned in some of these countries: The Philippines is a longtime ally. But American influence has often lagged that of China in Africa, Central Asia, Southeast Asia and even parts of South America in recent decades. That’s important to understanding key rudiments of US diplomacy today.

Focused on securing AI supply chains, Trump’s Pax Silica has built partnerships with Chile, Kazakhstan, Argentina, the Philippines and other countries. The US-backed Lobito Corridor, an infrastructure initiative connecting Angola to the DRC and Zambia, is meant to strengthen access to critical minerals.

The State Department is reportedly pushing Kazakhstan — which straddles Pax Silica and China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization — to make a sharper strategic choice. The initiatives are scattered, but the theme is clear: The map of US action and pressure is shifting in the age of AI.
Leaving US Allies Behind

A final challenge is ironic: AI will test the same alliance structure that gives Washington a position of tremendous strength. That network is already in turmoil amid long-building tensions over burden-sharing and the sharp, sometimes self-defeating controversies of Trump’s second term. Even as AI underscores the techno-strategic centrality of the US alliance structure, it will introduce new strains.

As the US lead over its allies at the frontier widens, there could be greater capability imbalances within NATO or other pacts — and greater uncertainty about whether Washington can be counted on to share access to top models with its friends. Persistent transatlantic differences over tech regulation could worsen as concerns about AI safety become more pronounced. AI could also stress the transatlantic alliance by forcing a rethink of which US allies matter most.

NATO has, historically, been the centerpiece of the US network. But the oil crises of the 1970s started to pull American focus toward the Persian Gulf. And as the world’s center of economic and military gravity has moved eastward, Washington has tried — not always successfully — to transfer attention and resources to the Pacific. A focus on AI could further decenter the old transatlantic core of the US security structure in favor of East Asia and the Persian Gulf.

So long as compute is king, the mighty “chiplands” of East Asia — Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, Singapore — will be vital to any AI-centric view of US alliances. In the Gulf, the UAE and Saudi Arabia command the energy resources and capital to quickly build AI infrastructure. Israel looms large, with its pioneering work on the military and intelligence applications of AI.

To be sure, some European countries — whether the Netherlands with its EUV dominance or Norway with its sovereign wealth fund — will be indispensable. The EU, thanks to the size of its market, will have influence in shaping AI governance norms. But Europe is hardly a hotbed of AI innovation; if its struggle continues, it will seem less important over time. In that scenario, tech advances will simply exacerbate a troubling transatlantic drift.
Technology Destroys Empires

Since ancient times, technological change has made and broken empires. It has reworked patterns of influence and advantage. The most recent great-power contest was decided, in part, by the move from one technological era to another. The Soviet Union was a superpower when strength resided in heavy industry and mass manufacturing. It was an also-ran amid the digital revolution that helped Washington and friends win the Cold War.

We don’t yet know whether AI will cause similar geopolitical earthquakes. Key components of that technology emerge from a geopolitical ecosystem that America has long cultivated. Success, from Washington’s perspective, involves using this advantage to lock in an extended period of US and democratic supremacy. Mastering a technological revolution is essential to preventing autocratic enemies from carrying out a geopolitical revolution of their own.

But AI will change the global landscape. It is revealing new relationships of power and dependence; it is remaking relations between non-state actors and states. It is highlighting the intersection of military danger and tech development in places from the Persian Gulf to the Taiwan Strait; it is challenging old views of which countries and regions matter most. The AI revolution is just beginning. But it will, undoubtedly, force us to revise our strategic maps in the years ahead.

examples.zh: 这份合同将把价格锁定两年。

annotations.explanation: carry out 常接计划、行动或变革。

target.text: But innovation continually remakes the world’s strategic geography — the meaning and value of key terrain.

annotations.translationZh: 然而，创新不断重塑世界的战略地理，也就是关键地域的意义和价值。
annotations.explanation: 主语是 innovation，谓语 remakes；破折号后的名词短语解释 strategic geography 的含义。

structure.text: the meaning and value of key terrain

target.text: The internal combustion engine made the Middle East a jackpot and a tinderbox.

annotations.translationZh: 内燃机使中东既成为财富宝地，也成为随时可能引爆冲突的火药桶。
annotations.explanation: make + 宾语 + 宾语补足语；jackpot 和 tinderbox 两个比喻分别指石油财富和冲突风险。

target.text: The development of AI challenges US diplomacy by highlighting the importance of areas Washington has underemphasized, such as Africa and South America — while also, paradoxically, straining some of the alliances that enhance America’s geo-technological power.

annotations.translationZh: AI 的发展凸显了非洲、南美等华盛顿此前重视不足地区的重要性，从而给美国外交带来挑战；同时，它又看似矛盾地使一些增强美国地缘技术实力的联盟承受压力。
annotations.explanation: areas 后省略关系代词的定语从句说明哪些地区被忽视；by highlighting 表方式，while also straining 表伴随或对照，that 从句修饰 alliances。

structure.text: by highlighting the importance of areas Washington has underemphasized

修饰 alliances 的定语从句

target.text: As AI capabilities race forward, so do fears of the havoc that poorly trained or rogue agents might create.

annotations.translationZh: 随着 AI 能力突飞猛进，人们对训练不足或失控代理可能造成严重破坏的担忧也在迅速增加。
annotations.explanation: As 引导随变化发展的状语从句；so do fears 为倒装，省略前文 race forward；that 从句修饰 havoc，that 是 create 的宾语。

structure.text: that poorly trained or rogue agents might create
structure.role: 修饰 havoc 的定语从句

annotations.explanation: So does ASML 承接前句 play crucial roles，表示 ASML 也发挥关键作用；as 说明其身份。

structure.text: as the world’s sole producer of EUV machines

target.text: Today, the US alliance system provides reliable access to many — not all — of the crucial inputs that drive America’s AI development, as well as leverage that helps it hold its rivals back.

annotations.translationZh: 如今，美国的联盟体系使其能够可靠地获得推动本国 AI 发展的许多关键投入品——但并非全部——同时也提供了帮助美国遏制竞争对手的影响力。
annotations.explanation: provides 的并列宾语为 access 和 leverage；两个 that 从句分别修饰 inputs 和 leverage；not all 为插入限定，强调并非完全自给。

structure.text: reliable access to many — not all — of the crucial inputs that drive America’s AI development
leverage that helps it hold its rivals back

annotations.translationZh: 这并不是一场势均力敌的竞争：北京在一定程度上通过对美国企业的成果进行逆向工程，使自己成为快速追赶者。
annotations.explanation: 冒号后解释前句判断；has made itself a fast follower 为宾语补足语结构，by reverse-engineering 表方式。此处是作者的评价。

structure.text: with the rest of the field far behind

annotations.explanation: 句首名词短语 + aside 表搁置某因素；inputs 后是省略关系代词的定语从句，inputs 是 access 的宾语。

structure.text: they must access through a contested world economy

annotations.explanation: prove attractive 表示事实证明有吸引力；not simply ... but also ... 连接两个地点成分；where 从句修饰 advanced economies；open-weight 指开放模型权重，不必然等于全面开源。

annotations.explanation: be poised to 表即将发生；by shifting 表方式；how 从句作 shifting 的宾语，involving ... 是修饰 interactions 的分词短语。

structure.text: is poised to unsettle the landscape of power
by shifting how interactions involving both state and non-state actors play out
involving both state and non-state actors

annotations.explanation: raising ... 为现在分词短语，说明前述位置带来的结果；technological cost 指对技术体系的损害和代价，不只是武器价格。
